Latent class (finite mixture) models for panel data

Source: R/fmm.R
panfmm.Rd

Finite mixture regression in which every individual belongs to one of k latent classes for all of its observations, the panel latent class model of Deb and Trivedi (1997, 2002) and Bago d'Uva (2006). Within class c the outcome follows a GLM with class-specific coefficients beta_c (and dispersion), and the individual likelihood is L_i = sum_c pi_ic prod_t f_c(y_it | x_it). Class probabilities are constant (pi_c) or depend on individual-level concomitant variables through a multinomial logit. In health economics the classes typically separate a large group of low users of care from a smaller group of high users with a different response to income, insurance or health status.

Usage

panfmm(
  formula,
  data,
  index,
  k = 2,
  family = "poisson",
  concomitant = NULL,
  nstart = 10,
  seed = NULL,
  vcov = c("classical", "cluster"),
  maxit = 1000,
  tol = 1e-06,
  na.action = stats::na.omit,
  weights = NULL,
  offset = NULL
)

Arguments

formula

a model formula y ~ x1 + x2 for the class-specific regressions (the same regressors in every class). It may contain offset() terms, e.g. offset(log(exposure)) for counts over different exposure periods; the offset enters the linear predictor of every class with coefficient 1. lag(x, k), lead(x, k) and diff(x) are taken within each individual on the grid of sorted distinct time values (needs index = c(id, time)); the first waves of each individual get NA and leave the sample, and lag(x, 0:2) gives several lags

data

a data.frame in long format

index

length-1 or length-2 character vector giving the individual (and time) columns; class membership is constant within individual. Use a row identifier for cross-section data

k

number of latent classes

family

"poisson", "negbin" (NB2), "gaussian", "binomial" (logit) or "probit" (binomial with probit link), or the corresponding panglm family spec, e.g. binomialfamily("probit")

concomitant

optional one-sided formula ~ z1 + z2 of individual-level (time-invariant) variables for the class probabilities

nstart

number of EM starts (the first deterministic, the others random)

seed

optional random seed for the random starts; the global random number stream is restored afterwards

vcov

"classical" (inverse negative Hessian) or "cluster" (sandwich clustered by individual); see vcov.panfmm()

maxit

maximum number of EM iterations per start

tol

convergence tolerance on the relative change of the EM log-likelihood

na.action

missing-data action passed to stats::model.frame()

weights

optional nonnegative individual (sampling) weights: the name of a column of data or a numeric vector with one value per row of data, constant within individuals; see the Weights section

offset

optional numeric offset (the name of a column of data or a vector with one value per row of data), added to the linear predictor of every class (in addition to any offset() terms of formula), as in stats::glm()

Value

an object of class "panfmm", a list with components coefficients (all parameters, named class<c>:<term> and prior<c>:<term>), vcov, vcov_type, classcoef (a matrix of class-specific regression coefficients, one column per class), sigma (Gaussian) or theta (NB2) by class, prior (the class probabilities of each individual, one row per individual; with no concomitant variables all rows are equal), prior_mean (their averages), posterior (posterior class probabilities, one row per individual, rownames the individual identifiers), class (the modal posterior class), classmean (the mean outcome of each class, used for the label order), loglik, df, starts (log-likelihood of each EM start), nobs, n_groups, weights (the individual weights, NULL without weights), offset (the total offset of each observation in panel order, NULL without offsets), k, family, call and formula. Methods: print, summary, coef, vcov, confint, predict, logLik (hence AIC and BIC, with n the number of observations), nobs, tidy and glance.

Estimation

The EM algorithm is run from nstart starting partitions of the individuals: the first splits them by the quantiles of their mean outcome, the others are random. The E step computes the posterior class probabilities tau_ic of each individual from the whole history y_i1, ..., y_iT; the M step fits one weighted GLM per class (weights tau_ic repeated over the individual's observations, iteratively reweighted least squares warm-started at the previous iteration's coefficients; NB2 by IRLS and a Newton step for theta) and the class probabilities (sample means of tau_ic, or a weighted multinomial logit on the concomitant variables). The run with the largest log-likelihood is then polished by BFGS and Newton steps on the observed-data log-likelihood sum_i log L_i, whose numerical Hessian (from analytic scores) gives the classical covariance solve(-H). The cluster covariance is the sandwich B (sum_g s_g s_g') B with B = solve(-H), the individual scores s_i summed within clusters (the individual by default) and the factor G / (G - 1), the convention used in the rest of the package for likelihoods whose units are individuals.

Weights

Class membership is a property of the individual, so weights are individual (sampling) weights: they must be constant within individuals (one weight per individual, repeated over its rows) and panfmm() stops otherwise. The fit maximizes the weighted pseudo log-likelihood sum_i w_i log L_i, the convention of flexmix (whose integer weights must also be identical within groups). In the EM algorithm the M step weights become w_i tau_ic, and the class probabilities are weighted means of the posteriors. The classical covariance is solve(-H_w) from the weighted Hessian, which is correct for frequency weights; for sampling weights use vcov = "cluster", the sandwich B (sum_g S_g S_g') B with the weighted individual scores S_i = w_i s_i summed within clusters. Individuals with zero weight do not contribute. With weights the reported loglik (hence AIC and BIC) is the weighted log-likelihood, and BIC keeps n the number of observations (flexmix uses the sum of the weights, which differs for sampling weights scaled to population totals).

Ancillary parameters are estimated on the log scale: log(sigma) for the Gaussian family and log(theta) for NB2 (variance mu + mu^2 / theta, i.e. alpha = 1 / theta). The class probabilities are parameterized by the multinomial logit coefficients of classes 2, ..., k against class 1 (an intercept only when there are no concomitant variables), and these are the parameters reported in coef() and vcov(); the implied probabilities are in fit$prior.

Label switching

Mixture likelihoods are invariant to permutations of the class labels. panfmm() orders the classes by ascending mean outcome: the mean over all observations of the class-specific fitted mean mu_c(x_it), so that class 1 is the low-use class and class k the high-use class. The multinomial logit of the class probabilities uses class 1 as reference.

Validation

Checked against flexmix in the package's validation suite on GitHub: flexmix::flexmix() with the | id grouping, started from the same posterior, gives the same log-likelihood, class and concomitant coefficients, class probabilities, posteriors and BIC, and flexmix::refit() the same standard errors, for Gaussian, Poisson, NB2 and binomial components; flexmix from its own random starts finds no better optimum.

References

Deb, P. and Trivedi, P. K. (1997). Demand for medical care by the elderly: a finite mixture approach. Journal of Applied Econometrics, 12, 313-336.

Deb, P. and Trivedi, P. K. (2002). The structure of demand for health care: latent class versus two-part models. Journal of Health Economics, 21, 601-625. doi:10.1016/S0167-6296(02)00008-5

Bago d'Uva, T. (2006). Latent class models for utilisation of health care. Health Economics, 15, 329-343. doi:10.1002/hec.1112

Gruen, B. and Leisch, F. (2008). FlexMix version 2: finite mixtures with concomitant variables and varying and constant parameters. Journal of Statistical Software, 28(4). doi:10.18637/jss.v028.i04

See also

summary.panfmm(), vcov.panfmm() and predict.panfmm() for the fitted model, tidy-methods for tidy() and glance().

Other panel models: panfmmselect(), panglm(), pangmm(), panhurdle(), paniv(), panqr(), panselect(), twopart()

Examples

# Doctor visits of 400 patients over 4 years: 70% low users and 30%
# high users with a stronger effect of chronic illness
set.seed(1)
N <- 400; TT <- 4
d <- data.frame(id = rep(seq_len(N), each = TT), year = rep(seq_len(TT), N))
high <- rep(rbinom(N, 1, 0.3), each = TT)
d$chronic <- rbinom(N * TT, 1, 0.4)
d$age <- rep(round(runif(N, 40, 80)), each = TT)
mu <- exp(ifelse(high == 1, 1.5 + 0.6 * d$chronic, 0 + 0.3 * d$chronic) +
          0.01 * (d$age - 60))
d$visits <- rpois(N * TT, mu)

fit <- panfmm(visits ~ chronic + age, data = d, index = c("id", "year"),
              k = 2, family = "poisson", nstart = 3, seed = 1)
summary(fit)
